title: Generative AI Use in the Legal Profession: Findings from the 2025 Victorian Lawyer Census

author: VLSB+C Legal Services Research Centre · Nigel Balmer

st.t: AI governance: Literacy and benchmarking build capacity
st.an: The supplied source material is bibliographic only and contains no substantive census findings, arguments, predictions or recommendations. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine whether the source supports, extends, redirects or opposes the cluster’s governance, literacy, benchmarking and human-oversight propositions.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliographic references only. Although they identify works concerning access to justice, unequal legal services and AI risks, they provide no census findings or authorial argument establishing whether the source accepts the cluster’s proposition that cheaper AI assistance may increase participation without improving remedies.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The supplied source excerpt contains no substantive claims, findings, reasoning or recommendations. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to assess its position on whether human oversight delivers effective control, requires independent verification, protects expertise development or is adequately governed by existing professional rules.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied source material contains only bibliographic references and provides no findings, reasoning, predictions or recommendations attributable to the source. It is therefore insufficient to determine whether the source supports or challenges the cluster’s account of AI redistributing legal tasks, status and professional power.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core balance: AI can improve accessibility and provider capacity through bounded, human-supervised uses, but efficiency gains do not automatically improve client outcomes and may reinforce inequity without governance and targeted support. It materially extends the synthesis with Victorian census evidence on uneven adoption, verification practices, guidance gaps and the need to prioritise under-resourced providers, while not directly measuring consumer outcomes.
qs: Without intervention to broaden how risks are managed, benefits are conceived, and to whom they flow, the use of AI risks reinforcing existing inequities rather than reducing them.

Notwithstanding AI’s      documented limitations, there is scope for it to enhance quality, accessibility      and affordability – for example, by translating complex legal concepts in ways      accessible to lay clients, enhancing triage and intake processes, providing      quality and completeness checks alongside human oversight, or enabling      service unbundling for those of limited means.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core framing and materially extends it with Victorian census evidence: lawyers primarily perceive efficiency gains, while adoption is uneven and safeguards, guidance and training remain incomplete. It also directly raises—but does not claim to prove—competence and professional-development risks from newer lawyers’ reliance on general-purpose AI.
qs: ‘Enhanced efficiency and productivity’ was the only proposed benefit for which a majority of respondents agreed or strongly agreed (71.3%).

While users generally appear aware of quality limitations and report taking steps to mitigate them, patterns of use raise questions about whether AI-assisted practice may undermine the development or retention of core professional skills.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The census accepts the need for active professional governance and materially extends the cluster with empirical evidence that governance capacity varies by practice setting and that enterprise AI policies can conflict with lawyers’ professional obligations. It also identifies unresolved accountability and client-benefit questions, reinforcing the case for targeted scrutiny rather than blanket reliability rules.
qs: These questions become particularly salient when considering the varying capacities across different practice settings to evaluate, implement and benefit from AI technologies.11 The legal profession’s relationship with technological change has long been complex.12 Professional obligations around confidentiality, competence and client service create considerations for evaluating new technologies.

Regarding conduct, it is observed that lawyers working outside traditional legal practice settings – in-house, for non-legal employers, or within incorporated practices – may face particular tensions where enterprise-level AI guidelines are not adequately attuned to legal-specific professional obligations, or position these obligations in conflict with organisational objectives.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The census accepts the supervised-use framing and materially extends it with empirical evidence from Victorian lawyers: most AI users report accuracy safeguards, while respondents and cited experiments recognise efficiency gains more consistently than quality gains. It also identifies practical governance, training and guidance gaps that affect safe deployment.
qs: Among those who did use AI, the majority (88.7%) reported taking steps to ensure accuracy.

Experimental work      suggests these tools can deliver efficiency gains, with studies finding that law      students using GPT-4 completed legal analysis tasks significantly faster than      those working without AI assistance.5 Yet the evidence on quality improvements      remains mixed.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-supervised deployment and adds concrete census evidence that current use is concentrated in information gathering, drafting and administration rather than legal decision-making. It materially extends the proposition by identifying uneven organisational capacity as an implementation constraint and recommending targeted support for safe evaluation and integration, especially in under-resourced settings.
qs: Consequently the most common forms of use were in the      areas of information-gathering, drafting and administration, rather than on      legal decision-making or the production of court documents.
What      is needed is effort to expand understanding of AI’s potential beyond efficiency      and to equip resource-constrained organisations to evaluate and implement      these tools safely.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The census supports the cluster’s bounded, implementation-focused account: adoption is uneven, use concentrates on lower-risk research, drafting and administrative tasks, and perceived efficiency benefits are accompanied by accuracy, privacy, security, training and governance concerns. Its self-reported practices and attitudes do not establish measured performance or investment value.
qs: Consequently the most common forms of use were in the      areas of information-gathering, drafting and administration, rather than on      legal decision-making or the production of court documents.
Perceived risks and benefits Accuracy, privacy and security were the most widely recognised risks.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between faster AI-assisted work and dependable legal performance. It reports significant time savings but mixed quality gains, stresses that speed to an acceptable quality threshold was not measured, and identifies unresolved accuracy and professional risks; it does not establish autonomous-lawyering reliability.
qs: Experimental work      suggests these tools can deliver efficiency gains, with studies finding that law      students using GPT-4 completed legal analysis tasks significantly faster than      those working without AI assistance.5 Yet the evidence on quality improvements      remains mixed.

Crucially, the research did not examine speed-to-      quality-threshold, which is arguably what matters most in practice.6      These uncertain quality outcomes are particularly troubling given the distinct      risks that accompany democratisation.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s account that fabricated AI citations have prompted differing judicial responses, including sanctions and warnings without sanctions. Its excerpts provide contextual incident and professional-rule references, but do not independently develop the cluster’s broader claims about verification standards, genuine-but-misleading authorities, or empirical error rates.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source provides limited but consistent support: it documents sanctions and judicial warnings involving AI-generated false citations, while distinguishing an incident that ended without sanctions. This aligns with the cluster’s treatment of hallucination cases as concrete incidents rather than general reliability measurements, and of sanctions as circumstance-dependent rather than automatic for AI use.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s premise that lower-cost, widely available generative AI can broaden access beyond well-resourced legal practices. Its support is limited to availability and historical market concentration; it does not show improved legal outcomes or address the cluster’s central protection, accountability and UPL concerns.
qs: Their low or no cost offering, wide availability and minimal barriers to entry essentially democratise access to sophisticated AI-powered tools.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source aligns closely with the cluster: it reports clear task-completion speed gains but mixed and inconsistent quality effects, argues that speed-to-quality-threshold is the more practical measure, and highlights reliability, competence, confidentiality and hallucination risks. It does not directly quantify verification costs, but supports the proposition that practical value depends on whether users can detect and manage uncertain output quality.
qs: Experimental work      suggests these tools can deliver efficiency gains, with studies finding that law      students using GPT-4 completed legal analysis tasks significantly faster than      those working without AI assistance.5 Yet the evidence on quality improvements      remains mixed.

Crucially, the research did not examine speed-to-      quality-threshold, which is arguably what matters most in practice.6      These uncertain quality outcomes are particularly troubling given the distinct      risks that accompany democratisation.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that demonstrated efficiency gains do not establish reliable legal quality or net practical value. It highlights inconsistent quality gains, unguaranteed accuracy, professional risks and the unresolved question of whether AI reaches an acceptable quality threshold faster, though it does not directly analyse verification as the required mitigation.
qs: Crucially, the research did not examine speed-to-      quality-threshold, which is arguably what matters most in practice.6      These uncertain quality outcomes are particularly troubling given the distinct      risks that accompany democratisation.

General-purpose AI systems rely on training      data that remains largely opaque with potential biases that are difficult to      identify, and accuracy that cannot be reliably guaranteed.7 Low barriers to entry      enable adoption by those who may lack the expertise to recognise these      limitations or develop effective prompts.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The census supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition by showing that legal AI adoption remains limited and is constrained by privacy, security, guidance and training concerns. Its contribution is descriptive rather than evaluative: it does not test reliability, service outcomes or particular legal-engineering solutions.

kp.k: Weighted voluntary census provides the empirical basis
kp.d: The report analyses a voluntary online survey of Victorian practising-certificate holders: 1,887 lawyers responded from 29,537 eligible holders, a 6.4% response rate. All analyses use post-stratification weights based on age, gender and certificate type. The questionnaire focused on reported use of AI tools; the report cautions that incidental or tacit use through search engines and embedded software may not be captured.
qs: The 2025 census was a voluntary online survey distributed to all Victorian lawyers holding practising certificates, with a total of 1,887 lawyers responding.
Of a total of 29,537 current practising certificate holders, a response rate of 6.4%.
It is also possible that some use is tacit, as AI becomes increasingly embedded in search engines and other software.

kp.k: Adoption remains partial and varies by career stage
kp.d: In the 2025 census, 36.7% reported AI use in legal practice; the detailed analysis identifies 638 users among 1,739 respondents answering yes or no. Among 607 users reporting frequency, 25% used AI daily, 35% weekly, 33% occasionally and 7% monthly. Adoption was 48.7% among those under 30 and 21.3% among those aged 70 or older. Those holding certificates for less than five years reported 41.7% adoption versus 30.7% for 20 or more years. Respondents speaking a language other than English at home reported 47.7% adoption versus 36.7% for English speakers.
qs: Just over one third (36.7%) of respondents reported using AI tools in their legal practice, with over half of these doing so daily or weekly.

This same pattern was also reflected in rates of use relative to the number of years a practising certificate had been held, with more experienced (and therefore often older) respondents exhibiting lower rates of adoption compared to newer (often younger) entrants to the profession.

kp.k: Organisational settings exhibit substantial adoption disparities
kp.d: Adoption was highest among non-legal employers (53.9%), incorporated legal practices (48.3%) and law firms (46.0%), compared with sole practitioners (24.4%), community-sector workers (26.7%) and government employers (11.6%). Certificate categories also differed: corporate legal practitioners reported 51.8%, barristers 14.6% and government legal practitioners 11.2%. In-house respondents overall reported 40.6%, versus 35.8% for others. Partnership status showed virtually no difference. These are distinct organisational, certificate and role classifications.
qs: Variations in adoption by partnership status were minimal (40% among partners and 40% among non-partners), although adoption by in-house lawyers was slightly higher (41%) compared to those who did not work in-house (36%).

More substantial variations in adoption were observed by organisation type, with those working for non-legal employers (54%), incorporated legal practices (48%) and law firms (46%) reporting the highest rates of use, while sole practitioners (24%), community sector workers (27%) and government employees (12%) reported the lowest.

kp.k: Practice-area adoption tracks perceived task suitability
kp.d: Table 2 reports adoption of 61.4% in IT/telecommunications, 58.9% in trade practice, 53.7% in intellectual property, 53.1% in small business and 50.0% in corporate law, versus 20.2% in criminal law, 24.3% in administrative law and 26.3% in advocacy. The authors suggest that higher uptake reflects alignment between AI's information-processing strengths and daily work. Lower adoption in relationship-intensive practices or those serving vulnerable clients may represent a rational assessment of current utility rather than failed uptake.
qs: And adoption concentrates in practice areas where AI’s current strengths (processing and synthesising natural language and numeric data) map most clearly to day-to-day work: IT/telecommunications, trade practices, intellectual property, and higher-volume transactional fields like commercial and corporate law.
This may not indicate a failure of uptake but rather a rational assessment of where general-purpose AI tools currently add value.

kp.k: General-purpose tools dominate over legal-specific products
kp.d: General-purpose tools accounted for 64.8% of reported use in the key findings, rounded to 65% in Table 3. Microsoft 365 Copilot was used by 34%, custom software and LEAP by 13% each, Lexis+ AI by 12%, JADE Professional by 9%, and Westlaw Precision/CoCounsel by 5%. Harvey.ai appears among tools volunteered in other responses, without a separate adoption estimate. The report contrasts readily accessible general-purpose models with legal-specific applications constrained to vetted legal resources.
qs: General-purpose AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot, were by far the most widely used (64.8%), with commercially available legal AI tools attracting far lower rates of use.
Their low or no cost offering, wide availability and minimal barriers to entry essentially democratise access to sophisticated AI-powered tools.

kp.k: Current uses emphasise research, communication and administration
kp.d: Among AI users, reported applications included background research on non-legal issues (44%), legal research and case analysis (40%), client communication (35%), document review and management (27%), transcription and note-taking (26%), and contract analysis and drafting other relevant documents (17%). Court-document preparation was reported by 6%, and case prediction or litigation outcomes by 1%; these uses were more common among litigation practitioners. Other reported uses included editing, administrative support, marketing, brainstorming and training preparation.
qs: As shown, background research on relevant non-legal issues was cited by the greater proportion of respondents (44%), followed by legal research and case analysis (40%) and client communication (35%).
Consequently the most common forms of use were in the areas of information-gathering, drafting and administration, rather than on legal decision-making or the production of court documents.

kp.k: Privacy and governance are leading adoption barriers
kp.d: Among non-users, 45% cited data, privacy and security concerns, 32% cited absent clear legal and ethical guidelines, and 21.8% reported workplace bans. Free-text responses described incomplete internal governance, uncertainty about approved tools, implementation delays, insufficient time, unreliable outputs and limited usefulness for judgment or direct client interaction. Some respondents also opposed AI because of environmental impacts, copyright concerns or perceived threats to young lawyers' jobs; these are respondents' views rather than measured effects.
qs: For almost half of respondents (45%), the decision not to use AI was a function of data, privacy and security concerns, followed by the absence of clear legal and ethical guidelines (32%).
When resources are scarce, prohibition may become a default response, as evidenced by the 21.8% of non-users who reported workplace bans on AI.
AI is taking away young lawyers’ jobs. I couldn’t in good conscience participate in its use.

kp.k: Most users report human verification and other safeguards
kp.d: The key findings report that 88.7% of users took steps to ensure accuracy. The detailed analysis reports 76% cross-checking legal accuracy against other sources, nearly half (reported as 50%) checking against hallucinations, 32% consulting colleagues or experts, and 11% comparing multiple AI tools. Other safeguards included personal review, professional judgment, restricting use to low-risk tasks and asking for sources. One non-user argued that verification consumed the time needed to do the original work. These findings describe reported practices, not tested safeguard effectiveness.
qs: Among those who did use AI, the majority (88.7%) reported taking steps to ensure accuracy.
As shown, 76% of users reported cross-checking the legal accuracy of output against other sources.
the time taken to check it for accuracy is the time I could have just done it myself originally
treating AI as a junior employee who needs supervision

kp.k: Training is widespread but insufficient as an isolated enabler
kp.d: Half of respondents had received AI training in the past year, including 72.3% of users and 37.6% of non-users. Lack of knowledge or training contributed to non-use for at least 328 respondents, but only 89 cited it alone. Seventy per cent wanted further training or materials, including 77% of users and 64% of non-users. Among those interested, workflow and efficiency (74%) and safe and ethical use (70%) led demand; users showed more interest in prompt writing, while non-users favoured foundational understanding and product assessment.
qs: Half of all respondents had received AI training in the past year, though rates were much higher among users (72.3%) than non-users (37.6%).

Yet further analysis revealed that only 89 of these attributed their non-use to a lack of training or knowledge alone, meaning that a lack of training and knowledge accounted for relatively little non-use in isolation.
Interest was strongest for training on how AI can enhance workflow and efficiency (74%), followed closely by the safe and ethical use of AI (70%).

kp.k: Professional guidance has limited reach despite workplace policies
kp.d: Twenty-nine per cent had read the Supreme and County Court guidelines, 29% the VLSB+C statement, 18.4% both, and 60% neither. Among AI users, 50% had read at least one document. Workplace guidelines existed for 42% overall; among users, 63% reported guidelines, 31% reported none and 7% were unsure. In-house counsel reported workplace guidelines more often than other lawyers (60% versus 37%). The report identifies uncertainty about policies as a possible compliance risk.
qs: Few respondents reported having read both documents (18.4%) with the majority having read neither document (60%).
Of those using AI, 63% were using them in workplaces where AI guidelines existed, compared to 31% who were using them in the absence of workplace guidelines.
In-house counsel also reported higher rates of workplace AI guidelines compared to other lawyer types (60% vs 37%).

kp.k: Lawyers strongly endorse duties, training and disclosure
kp.d: The key findings report 95.5% agreement that AI use must comply with professional obligations. In the detailed findings, 79% supported training for all lawyers, 63% disclosure to clients and 68% disclosure in litigation. Fifty-three per cent considered effective AI use necessary to modern legal practice, despite only 37% reporting use; 18% thought lawyers should not use AI. Non-users supported disclosure more strongly and expressed greater opposition to use. These are professional attitudes, not statements of enacted disclosure or training requirements.
qs: There was very strong agreement (95.5%) that lawyers have a duty to ensure AI use complies with professional obligations.
Most respondents also indicated that use should be disclosed to both clients (63% agreeing or strongly agreeing) or when used in litigation (68% agreeing or strongly agreeing).
A small, yet significant percentage (18%) felt that lawyers should not use AI.

kp.k: Efficiency dominates benefits; job replacement ranks lowest among risks
kp.d: Accuracy, privacy and security were the leading perceived risks; non-users expressed greater concern on individual risk dimensions except data inaccuracy. Only 36%, excluding don't-know responses, regarded job replacement as a significant threat, the lowest-ranked risk. Efficiency and productivity attracted 71.3% support in the key findings and were the sole benefit with majority agreement. The discussion reports affordability at 46%, accessibility at 45%, work quality at 31% and client satisfaction at 26%. These are perceptions, not measured productivity, employment or client outcomes.
qs: Notably, fears about AI replacing lawyers ranked lowest among perceived risks, with only 36% of respondents (excluding ‘don’t know’ responses) agreeing or strongly agreeing that this represented a significant threat.
‘Enhanced efficiency and productivity’ was the only proposed benefit for which a majority of respondents agreed or strongly agreed (71.3%).
Yet far fewer saw AI as enhancing affordability (46%), accessibility (45%), quality (31%) or client satisfaction (26%).

kp.k: Composite scores link adoption more strongly with perceived benefits
kp.d: Principal components analysis reduced eight risk items and six benefit items to separate standardised factors, with zero representing the sample average. Users had risk and benefit scores of 0.08 and 0.46, versus -0.07 and -0.25 for non-users. Daily users had the highest frequency-group scores for both risk (0.25) and benefit (0.87). Court-document users scored 0.39 for risk and 0.71 for benefit; contract-analysis and drafting users scored 0.24 and 0.73. Training and workplace guidance were associated with higher benefit perceptions and relatively little change in risk. The authors acknowledge that the measures would benefit from deeper psychometric analysis.
qs: Use of AI was associated with far greater perceived benefits and little change in perceived risks.
Interestingly, those using AI most frequently also had the highest perceived risk scores.
However, the items would benefit from more in-depth psychometric analysis

kp.k: Authors interpret adoption through utility and organisational capacity
kp.d: The report argues that perceived utility primarily shapes adoption, moderated by organisational context and capacity. It interprets higher perceived benefits alongside tolerated risk as an expected-value threshold, rather than risk avoidance alone. Under-resourced organisations may lack evaluation and implementation capacity. For in-house, government and non-legal-employer lawyers, adoption decisions may instead occur at enterprise level. The report explicitly allows that senior non-users' caution may reflect informed professional judgment rather than technological unfamiliarity.
qs: The data suggests that adoption is shaped primarily by perceived utility, that is, whether a lawyer sees a clear benefit from AI in the context of their specific work.
Conversely, low perceived risk does not drive adoption where perceived benefit is also low.

And for in-house lawyers, those with non-legal employers, and those in government settings, the decision to adopt may not rest with the individual lawyer or even the legal team, but instead occur at the level of organisational strategy, where risks and benefits are evaluated in aggregate against broader operational objectives.

kp.k: Efficiency gains may not translate into client value
kp.d: The authors warn of an efficiency trap: productivity gains could become higher provider profits rather than lower client fees, while a dominant efficiency narrative narrows experimentation and training. They also raise a conditional concern that accepting speed without quality improvement could conceal quality trade-offs. These are interpretations and prospective risks, not observed pricing or profit changes. The report's review of external law-student experiments finds faster legal analysis with GPT-4 but mixed quality gains and no examination of speed-to-quality-threshold.
qs: This risks an outcome in which productivity improvements translate to higher profits rather than lower fees.
If practitioners only expect speed or productivity improvements, that is all they will look for, and the dominance of the efficiency narrative risks that narrative becoming self-reinforcing.
The same study found that while lower-skilled participants saw some quality improvements on certain tasks, these gains were neither consistent nor universal.

kp.k: Junior adoption raises unresolved professional formation concerns
kp.d: The report states that general-purpose AI use extending into legal analysis and application is concentrated among newer entrants. Although users report risk mitigation, the authors question whether AI assistance could undermine core skill acquisition or retention. They invoke research from other domains on cognitive offloading, learning, recall and creativity as grounds for concern; the census does not establish deterioration in lawyers' competence.
qs: General-purpose AI tool use, particularly for tasks extending beyond information gathering to legal analysis and application, is concentrated among newer entrants to the profession.

While users generally appear aware of quality limitations and report taking steps to mitigate them, patterns of use raise questions about whether AI-assisted practice may undermine the development or retention of core professional skills.

kp.k: Enterprise AI policies may conflict with legal obligations
kp.d: The authors identify potential conduct tensions for in-house lawyers, lawyers employed by non-legal organisations and those in incorporated practices. General-workforce AI policies may inadequately address legal-specific duties or prioritise conflicting organisational objectives. Limited awareness of court and regulator guidance could leave these tensions unnoticed. Broader dissemination is proposed both to improve compliance among users and reduce hesitation among non-users who perceive a lack of guidance.
qs: Where workplace guidelines exist – and they are more common in settings with higher adoption, such as in-house roles and non-legal employers – they may be designed for general workforces rather than legal professionals specifically.
Without awareness of court and regulator guidance, lawyers in these settings risk compliance failures where workplace policies diverge from professional obligations.

That a third of non-users cited the absence of legal and ethical guidelines as a barrier to adoption suggests that broader awareness could both improve compliance among users and reduce unnecessary hesitation among non-users.

kp.k: Targeted support should broaden access-to-justice benefits
kp.d: The report recommends moving beyond workflow optimisation toward safe integration and demonstrable consumer benefits, especially in community legal services, small practices and sole practice. Suggested applications include explaining complex legal concepts to lay clients, improving triage and intake, human-supervised completeness checks and unbundled services for people of limited means; these are opportunities rather than demonstrated census outcomes. Proposed regulatory support includes practice-specific policy and risk-assessment templates, guidance awareness, capacity building and grants. The authors argue that environmental and societal costs cannot be justified solely by concentrated efficiency gains for well-resourced providers.
qs: The greatest need for support is likely to arise in under-resourced settings (community legal services, small practices and sole practitioners) where lawyers face the most acute mismatch between demands and resources.
If the environmental and societal costs of AI are to be justified at all, it cannot be on the basis of concentrated efficiency gains for well-resourced providers.

There is value in the VLSB+C considering how it might raise awareness of different use cases, make implementation tools available (such as templates for workplace guidelines or risk assessments) for different areas of practice, and support capacity building where it is most needed, for example through grants that enable the potential of AI to be realised and its benefits made available for a wider range of stakeholders.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI adoption is uneven and currently centres on assistance with research, drafting and administration rather than legal decision-making.
pts.d: The VLSB+C Legal Services Research Centre reports that 36.7% of respondents used AI in practice in 2025; among users answering the frequency question, 35% used it weekly and 25% daily. General-purpose tools dominated use (approximately 65% of users), ahead of Microsoft 365 Copilot (34%) and individual legal-specific products. Reported applications included non-legal background research (44%), legal research and case analysis (40%), client communication (35%), document review (27%) and transcription (26%); court-document preparation (6%) and case prediction (1%) were much rarer. These findings describe reported use, not autonomous delivery of legal services.

pts.k: Low-cost general-purpose AI broadens access to technology, but observed adoption depends on perceived usefulness and organisational capacity.
pts.d: The report contrasts widely available general-purpose models with earlier specialist legal technologies concentrated in well-resourced commercial firms. It interprets the census as suggesting that perceived benefits, moderated by organisational context, drive adoption more than low perceived risk alone. Higher uptake among younger lawyers, speakers of languages other than English at home and transactional or technology-related practices is interpreted as reflecting task-specific utility. Lower uptake in relationship-intensive practices may be a rational assessment of current usefulness, while scarce implementation resources and enterprise decisions may constrain adoption elsewhere. These explanations are the report's interpretations of associations, rather than demonstrated causal effects.

pts.k: Efficiency is AI's dominant perceived benefit, but faster work does not necessarily improve quality or client outcomes.
pts.d: The report finds that 71.3% perceived efficiency and productivity benefits, compared with 46% for affordability, 45% for accessibility, 31% for quality and 26% for client satisfaction. It cites experimental research by Choi and colleagues in which law students using GPT-4 completed legal-analysis tasks faster, while quality gains were mixed and concentrated in some tasks among lower-skilled participants. The report warns that provider-focused efficiency could become self-reinforcing and translate into greater profits rather than lower fees. It presents this distributional outcome as a risk inferred from attitudes and use patterns, not as a measured change in prices, profits or service quality.

pts.k: Accessible AI creates accuracy, confidentiality and verification burdens; most users report checking outputs.
pts.d: The report argues that low barriers to entry allow adoption by practitioners who may lack the expertise to recognise model limitations or prompt effectively. It identifies opaque training data, bias, fabricated legal information and confidentiality risks, particularly outside enterprise agreements. Among users answering the quality-assurance questions, approximately 89% reported accuracy safeguards: 76% cross-checked legal accuracy, approximately 50% checked for hallucinations and 32% consulted colleagues or experts. These are reported verification practices, not measurements of their effectiveness or of model error rates. The report cites sanctions incidents as evidence of realised professional consequences. Separately, an anonymous non-user argues that verification can erase time savings; that is the respondent's experience or assessment, not a census-wide finding.

pts.k: AI-assisted practice may impair the development and retention of core legal skills, particularly among newer entrants.
pts.d: The report raises a prospective competence concern because general-purpose AI use, including legal analysis and application, is concentrated among newer lawyers. It supports this concern with research from education and cognition concerning cognitive offloading, recall, problem-solving, retention and creative fixation. It does not report direct measurement of skill deterioration among Victorian lawyers. The cross-domain literature is offered as a reason for closer attention to professional development, not as a demonstrated legal-profession outcome.

pts.k: Enterprise AI policies can conflict with lawyers' professional duties, and limited awareness of professional guidance can increase compliance risks.
pts.d: The report warns particularly about in-house lawyers, lawyers employed by non-legal organisations and those in incorporated practices. Workplace AI policies may serve a general workforce or organisational objectives without adequately addressing legal obligations. Sixty per cent of respondents had read neither relevant court guidance nor the regulator's statement, including approximately half of AI users. The report suggests wider awareness could improve compliance and reduce unnecessary non-adoption. Training and workplace guidelines were associated with higher perceived benefits and comparatively small differences in perceived risk; this does not establish that training or guidance caused adoption or compliance improvements.

pts.k: Without targeted support, AI may reinforce legal-service inequities; broader applications could improve access to justice.
pts.d: The report argues that narrowly conceived efficiency benefits and uneven implementation capacity risk concentrating advantage among well-resourced providers. It identifies potential applications in explaining legal concepts to lay clients, triage and intake, human-supervised completeness checks and service unbundling for people of limited means. These are proposed opportunities, not evaluated interventions. It recommends support for under-resourced providers through safe-integration training, policy and risk-assessment templates, capacity building and potentially grants. It also makes a normative argument that AI's environmental and societal costs should be justified through demonstrable public-facing access-to-justice gains rather than concentrated provider efficiencies.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a weighted voluntary survey of Victorian lawyers; broader implications also draw on external studies, cases and interpretive argument.
pts.d: The 2026 report analyses the 2025 Victorian Lawyer Census: 1,887 responses from 29,537 practising-certificate holders, a 6.4% response rate. It weights responses by age, gender and certificate type using regulator records. The AI-use question had 1,739 yes/no responses, including 638 users; denominators vary across questions. Principal components analysis generated composite perceived-risk and perceived-benefit scores, with the report acknowledging a need for deeper psychometric analysis. The survey measures self-reported use, safeguards and perceptions, not actual productivity, fees, quality, employment displacement or client access outcomes. External support includes the GPT-4 law-student experiment, literature on model limitations and cognition, reporting on hallucination-related sanctions and scholarship on unequal access to legal technology. One respondent's claim that AI is taking young lawyers' jobs is an attributed opinion, while only 36% of respondents excluding 'don't know' responses regarded replacement as a significant threat; the report does not establish displacement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical findings are a 2025 snapshot; predictions about skills, compliance and inequality are conditional and have no specified deadline.
pts.d: Published in 2026, the report describes adoption at the time of the 2025 census, with training questions covering the preceding year. Its general-purpose AI context begins with ChatGPT's emergence in late 2022. It notes that explicit questions about 'AI tools' may miss incidental or tacit use embedded in other software. Potential future harms depend on factors such as reliance on AI for substantive work, inadequate quality control, policy conflicts and absent support for resource-constrained providers. Proposed access and quality benefits depend on safe implementation, human oversight and broader use-case development. The cited task-speed experiment did not assess time to reach a required quality threshold, and its quality improvements were neither consistent nor universal. No quantified adoption trajectory, displacement forecast or date for market transformation is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ by career stage, practice setting and client population, with particular concerns for newer lawyers and under-resourced services.
pts.d: Respondents under 30 reported 48.7% adoption, compared with 21.3% among those aged 70 or over; newer entrants are the focus of the skills-development concern. Speakers of a language other than English at home reported 47.7% adoption, compared with 36.7% among English-at-home respondents; communication assistance is a proposed explanation. Adoption was highest among respondents working for non-legal employers (53.9%), incorporated practices (48.3%) and law firms (46.0%), versus sole practitioners (24.4%), the community sector (26.7%) and government employers (11.6%). In-house lawyers, as the corporate buyer side, face possible tensions between enterprise objectives and professional duties. IT/telecommunications and trade-practice lawyers reported comparatively high uptake, while criminal and administrative lawyers reported low uptake. Clients, especially vulnerable people and those of limited means, may receive few benefits unless efficiency gains translate into affordability, accessible services and improved quality. The regulator is identified as a potential source of implementation support.
